brief.situation: 16:00 in an outpatient pediatric clinic. You are the physical therapist. Leo, 6, was referred by his pediatrician for 'knee pain, likely growing pains, strengthening and agility'. His father says the limp comes and goes and is worse after soccer.
handover: No imaging has been done. No fever or recent illness.
Clinic policy: a child's limp with hip signs goes back to the pediatrician for hip X-rays and pediatric orthopedics the same week.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Each check takes the time on its button. Decide what the findings mean, what to stop or start, and who must know.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.label: What and why
parts.criteria: A 6-year-old boy with a limp, knee pain, a normal knee and lost, painful hip abduction and internal rotation suggests Legg-Calve-Perthes disease, avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
parts.modelAnswer: Not growing pains. He's a 6-year-old boy with a limp, his knee is normal, and his hip has lost abduction and internal rotation. That's Perthes until proven otherwise.

parts.label: What I do
parts.criteria: No impact or jumping; call the pediatrician for hip X-rays and pediatric orthopedics; explain activity limits; document.
parts.modelAnswer: No jumping or soccer, call the pediatrician for hip X-rays and orthopedics, and explain the limits to his dad.

scoring.modelReasoning: Legg-Calve-Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head, 3 to 5 times more common in boys, presenting with a limp and hip, groin or knee pain with lost abduction and internal rotation. Knee pain with a normal knee means examine the hip. Avoid impact, refer for hip X-rays and pediatric orthopedics, and explain activity limits.
